items.title: Five Levels, Five Feelings Released: Sorrow, Pain, Joy, Pleasure, and Equanimity Itself

items.zh: 復次，此四靜慮亦得名為出諸受事。謂初靜慮出離憂根，第二靜慮出離苦根，第三靜慮出離喜根，第四靜慮出離樂根，於無相中出離捨根。
items.en: Further, these four dhyānas may also be called the release of feeling. The first dhyāna releases the faculty of sorrow; the second dhyāna releases the faculty of pain; the third dhyāna releases the faculty of joy; the fourth dhyāna releases the faculty of pleasure; and within the signless concentration, the faculty of equanimity itself is released.

items.title: Diagnosing Sorrow While It's Happening: Cause, Condition, Origin, Mark, and Activity

items.zh: 如薄伽梵無倒經中說如是言：苾芻！憂根生已，應當如實了知生者。此於何位？謂即於此斷方便位，若為憂根間心相續，爾時應知。又應并此因、緣及序，若相，若行，皆如實知者。
items.en: As the Blessed One said in the Sūtra Free of Distortion: "Monastics, once the faculty of sorrow has arisen, it should be truly known as arisen." At what stage does this apply? It applies precisely at the stage of striving to sever sorrow — whenever sorrow interrupts the mind's own continuity, one should recognise it at that very moment. Further, its cause, its condition, its origin, its mark, and its activity should all likewise be truly known.

items.zh: 云何知因？謂了知此種子相續。云何知緣？謂了知此種所不攝所依、助伴。云何知序？謂知憂根託此事生，即是能發憂根之相及無知種子。云何知相？謂了知此是慼行相。云何知行？謂了知此能發之行，即不如理作意相應思也。
items.en: What is knowing its cause? Knowing that this sorrow's own seed continues on. What is knowing its condition? Knowing the basis and accompanying factors not already contained within that seed. What is knowing its origin? Knowing what specific occasion sorrow rests on to arise — namely, the mark that actually triggers it, together with the seed of ignorance behind it. What is knowing its mark? Knowing that this is grief's own characteristic feel. What is knowing its activity? Knowing the activity it drives — namely, intention associated with unsound reflection.

items.title: Restraining the Mind, Then Uprooting the Seed — Why Worldly Concentration Alone Never Finishes the Job

items.zh: 如是知已，於出離中極制持心者，云何制持？謂於染污行制攝其心，於思惟修任持堅住。又於是中，無餘盡滅乃至究竟者。謂滅隨眠故，滅諸纏故。
items.en: Having thus recognised it, how does one firmly restrain and hold the mind in the course of releasing it? By restraining and gathering the mind away from defiled activity, and by sustaining it, firmly held, in reflective cultivation. And what is meant by its being eliminated entirely, down to the very end? It means the latent tendency itself is eliminated, and its active manifestation is eliminated.

items.zh: 世間靜慮但能漸捨彼品麁重，不拔種子。若異此者，種永拔故，後不應生。無漏靜慮二種俱捨。如是於餘隨應當知。問：
items.en: Worldly meditative absorption can only gradually shed that category's own coarse unfitness; it cannot uproot the underlying seed. Were it otherwise — were the seed truly and permanently uprooted — it should never arise again afterwards. Uncontaminated meditative absorption discards both. The same should be understood, as applicable, for every other feeling-faculty as well.

items.title: Two Faces of Sorrow: Craving Denied, and the Anxious Longing for Liberation Not Yet Reached

items.zh: 以何等相了知憂根？答：或染污相、或出離欲俱行善相。
items.en: By what mark is the faculty of sorrow known? Answer: Either by a defiled mark, or by a wholesome mark accompanying the wish to be free of desire.

items.zh: 苦根者，或由自等增上力故，或由身勞增上力故，或火燒等增上力故，或他逼等增上力故，諸離欲者猶尚生起。喜根者，謂第二靜慮中，即第二靜慮地攝。樂根者，謂第三靜慮中，即第三靜慮地攝。問：
items.en: The faculty of pain arises through the dominant force of harm to oneself and the like, through the dominant force of bodily fatigue, through the dominant force of burning by fire and the like, or through the dominant force of harm inflicted by another — even one who has become free of desire still experiences this. The faculty of joy belongs to the second dhyāna, included within that level. The faculty of pleasure belongs to the third dhyāna, included within that level.

items.title: Why Pain's Seed Survives the First Dhyāna, Yet Never Manifests for a God Born There

items.zh: 何故苦根初靜慮中說未斷耶？答：彼品麁重猶未斷故。問：何緣生在初靜慮者苦根未斷而不現行？答：由其助伴相對憂根所攝諸苦彼已斷故。
items.en: Why is it said that pain is not yet severed even in the first dhyāna? Answer: Because that category's own coarse unfitness has not yet been severed. Then for what reason does one actually born in the first dhyāna not have pain manifest, even though it is not severed? Answer: Because the sufferings belonging to its companion and counterpart, the faculty of sorrow, have, for such a being, already been severed.

items.title: Proving the First Dhyāna Has Not Severed Pain — and How Each Higher Level Releases One Feeling in Turn

items.zh: 若初靜慮已斷苦根，是則行者入初靜慮及第二時，受所作住差別應無。由二俱有喜及樂故。而經中說：由出諸受，靜慮差別。又此應無尋伺寂靜麁重斷滅所作差別。如是餘根彼品麁重漸次斷故，上諸靜慮斷有差別。
items.en: If the first dhyāna had already severed pain, then when a practitioner enters the first dhyāna and again the second, there would be no difference in the feelings they produce and abide in — for both alike possess joy and pleasure. Yet the scriptures teach that the dhyānas are distinguished precisely by which feelings they release. Furthermore, on that supposition there would also be no difference made by the stilling of applied-and-sustained thought and the severing of its coarse unfitness. In this same way, because each category's coarse unfitness is severed by stages, the higher dhyānas differ in what they sever.

items.title: Equanimity's Release: The Signless Concentration Cuts the Seed, Not the Feeling Itself

items.zh: 又無相者，經中說為無相心定。於此定中捨根永滅，但害隨眠；彼品麁重無餘斷故。非滅現纏，住無相定必有受故。於此定中容有三受，謂喜、樂、捨。
items.en: As for the signless, the scriptures call it the signless mind-concentration. Within this concentration the equanimity-faculty is forever extinguished — yet only in the sense that its latent tendency is destroyed, because that category's coarse unfitness is severed without remainder. It is not that the present feeling is abolished, for one abiding in the signless concentration must still have feeling. Within this concentration three feelings may occur: joy, pleasure, and equanimity.

items.title: Why This Counts as "Severance," and How Far Equanimity Reaches

items.zh: 非彼諸受得有隨眠。煩惱斷故，說以為斷；彼品麁重說名隨眠。又此捨根乃至何處？當知始從第四靜慮乃至有頂。
items.en: It is not that these feelings themselves possess a latent tendency; rather, because the affliction is severed, it is called "severed" — the coarse unfitness of that category is what is termed the latent tendency. And how far does this equanimity-faculty extend? One should know that it runs from the fourth dhyāna all the way up to the peak of existence.

items.title: The Five Gateways of Favourable Release, and the Defilement Each One Answers

items.zh: 復次，此五根出離、無相為後，與彼五種順出離界展轉相攝。此中由欲、恚、害出離，即說乃至樂根出離；由色出離，即說第四靜慮捨根出離；由薩迦耶滅，即說無色界一切捨根出離。
items.en: Furthermore, this release of the five faculties — with the signless as the last — interlocks reciprocally with those five gateways of favourable release. Herein, from the release of desire, ill-will, and harm is said to follow the release running all the way up to the pleasure-faculty; from the release of form is said to follow the fourth dhyāna's release of the equanimity-faculty; and from the cessation of the view of a real self is said to follow the release of all equanimity in the formless realm.

items.title: What "Favourable Release" Actually Means — and Why Three Separate Antidotes for One Simultaneous Severance

items.zh: 順出離言有何等義？由住此者能出離故，名順出離。不說由此出離於彼。為離欲者說此界故。
items.en: What does the term "favourable release" mean? Because one who abides in these is able to be released, it is called favourable release. It is not being said that by means of these one is released from those; rather, this gateway is taught for the sake of one who is free of desire, the desire bound up with the perishable aggregates (satkāya).

items.zh: 問：諸欲、恚、害定同時斷，何緣建立別出離耶？答：彼諸出離雖復同時，約修對治有差別故，宣說三種出離差別。對治差別者，謂不淨、慈、悲，如其次第。或有唯修不淨出離一切；或慈、或悲。是故別說三種出離。
items.en: Question: Desire, ill-will, and harm are certainly severed at the same moment; on what grounds, then, is a separate release established for each? Answer: Although those releases are indeed simultaneous, because there is a difference in the antidote cultivated, three distinct releases are proclaimed. The difference in antidote is this: impurity, loving-kindness, and compassion, respectively. Some may cultivate the impurity contemplation alone and be released from all of them; or loving-kindness alone; or compassion alone. It is for this reason that three releases are stated separately.

items.title: One Antidote for the Higher Equanimity, and How to Test Whether Desire Is Truly Gone

items.zh: 此上唯有一類對治，故後出離無有差別。云何猛利見者等隨念欲？謂由觀察作意於勝事作意故，猛利功用作意故。
items.en: Above this, there is only one kind of antidote, so the later releases make no distinction. … What is it for a sharp-seeing one to call desires to mind, whether all together or one by one? It is by the attention of investigation directed at the excellent objects, and by an attention of fierce, forceful application.

blocks.text: Today's reading answers a precise question: at which level of meditation is each kind of feeling left behind? The answer distinguishes between a feeling not arising and its seed being cut. This is the difference between worldly meditation and the noble path, and the treatise makes it with great care.

"The first dhyāna releases the faculty of **sorrow**; the second, **pain**; the third, **joy**; the fourth, **pleasure**; and the signless concentration, **equanimity**." Venerable Miào Jìng explains "faculty" (根) here as dominance: each feeling is especially powerful in bringing something about.

The sūtra says to know sorrow's cause, condition, origin, mark, and activity. Master Cháng Bǎi on its mark: "brows locked, forehead knotted". This is meditation as diagnosis: see the feeling clearly while it happens, its cause and its effect, and it loses its hold.

Worldly concentration sheds the coarse unfitness of a feeling but cannot uproot its seed. Master Cháng Bǎi: "Worldly first dhyāna removes desire's manifestation, but its seed remains; when conditions come it manifests again and the dhyāna is lost." Only the noble path cuts seeds.

Sorrow is usually craving denied. But it can also have "a wholesome mark accompanying the wish to be free of desire". Master Cháng Bǎi: a practitioner who has meditated long without result grows sorrowful. This sorrow is not a fault; it can drive practice.

subs.head: Why pain survives the first dhyāna

blocks.text: Pain is "not yet severed even in the first dhyāna", because its own coarse unfitness has not been cut. Yet a god born in the first dhyāna never experiences pain. Venerable Miào Jìng: pain's "companion" is sorrow; with sorrow gone, pain has nothing to arise with. (Ru-Yi's translation reverses the relation; the teachers' reading is followed here.) The distinction is again between non-arising and severance: the first dhyāna cuts sorrow but not yet pain; only the second cuts pain.

Equanimity is released in the **signless concentration of mind** (無相心定), which cuts the seed of attachment to equanimity, not the feeling itself. Within that concentration, joy, pleasure, or equanimity may still occur; one simply no longer reacts to them with affliction. This is an important clarification about what liberation is: not the absence of feeling, but freedom within it.

These releases interlock with five **gateways of favourable release** (順出離界; Master Cháng Bǎi: 界 means cause). Release from desire, ill will, and harm leads up to release from pleasure; release from form, to the fourth dhyāna's equanimity; the cessation of self-view, to final release.

Desire, ill will, and harm are severed together. Why three releases, then? "Because there is a difference in the antidote cultivated": impurity, loving-kindness, compassion. One who cultivates any one well is released from all three.

"A sharp-seeing one calls desires to mind." Venerable Miào Jìng: this is a noble one, from stream-entry up, who deliberately calls up sense objects in calm to test whether desire is truly gone. Testing oneself is part of the path.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, which feeling does each level release?
options: first sorrow, second pain, third joy, fourth pleasure, and in the signless, equanimity
quiz.why: "The first dhyāna releases the faculty of sorrow; the second … pain; the third … joy; the fourth … pleasure; and within the signless concentration, the faculty of equanimity itself is released." Master Cháng Bǎi: ultimately all feeling is suffering; this is said of uncontaminated absorption.

quiz.q: The sūtra says to know sorrow's cause, condition, origin, mark, and activity. How does Master Cháng Bǎi describe its "mark"?
options: the look of grief — brows knit, forehead furrowed
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Knowing sorrow's appearance as grief — brows locked, forehead knotted." The text: "What is knowing its mark? Knowing that this is grief's own characteristic feel. What is knowing its activity? … intention associated with unsound reflection."

quiz.q: Worldly absorption sheds coarse unfitness but can't uproot seeds. What happens to someone with worldly first dhyāna, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: desire's manifestation is removed, but its seed remains; when conditions arise it manifests again and the dhyāna is lost
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Worldly first dhyāna removes desire's manifestation, but its seed remains; when conditions come it manifests again, and the dhyāna is lost." The text: "Uncontaminated meditative absorption discards both." Venerable Miào Jìng: worldly absorption is what non-Buddhists can also attain.

quiz.q: The text argues: if the first dhyāna cut pain, it wouldn't differ from the second. How does Venerable Miào Jìng state the difference?
options: the first cuts sorrow but not yet pain; only the second cuts pain
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "The difference is that the first dhyāna cuts sorrow but not yet pain; only the second cuts pain — there's the difference." Master Cháng Bǎi: from the second dhyāna up, headaches and aches are gone.

quiz.q: In the signless concentration equanimity is extinguished; is there still feeling? The note says only neutral feeling. What do the text and Master Cháng Bǎi say?
options: joy, pleasure, and equanimity may occur — one simply no longer reacts with affliction or is bound by feeling
quiz.why: "One abiding in the signless concentration must still have feeling. Within this concentration three feelings may occur: joy, pleasure, and equanimity." Master Cháng Bǎi: "Body and mind still have joy, pleasure, and equanimity." The note's "only neutral" is wrong (logged); what is extinguished is the latent tendency.

quiz.q: Desire, ill will, and harm are severed together — why three separate releases?
options: the antidotes differ — impurity, loving-kindness, compassion; some cultivate just one and are released from all
quiz.why: "Although those releases are indeed simultaneous, because there is a difference in the antidote cultivated, three distinct releases are proclaimed … impurity, loving-kindness, and compassion." Master Cháng Bǎi: temperaments differ — each suits a different contemplation.

quiz.q: "A sharp-seeing one calls desires to mind." Who is this, and why deliberately, per Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: noble ones from stream-entry up — deliberately calling up sense objects in calm to test whether desire is truly gone
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "This isn't an ordinary person — it's a noble one from stream-entry up"; "in calm, he deliberately contemplates worldly sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches." Master Cháng Bǎi: this confirms whether desire is gone, avoiding overestimation.
